questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
questions.context: When people are asked to rate an experience afterward, they do not average how they felt at every moment; they report something closer to the emotional intensity of the worst or best moment, combined with how the experience ended. A patient whose procedure ends with a period of mild, static discomfort rather than a peak of sharp pain will remember the whole experience as less unpleasant than a patient whose objectively shorter procedure ends abruptly at its most painful point. Duration barely registers at all. What is retained is a kind of highlight reel, edited severely and weighted heavily toward the final scene.

options.text: Why Longer Experiences Always Feel Worse in Memory
The Peak and the Ending: How Memory Distorts Experience
A Guide to Reducing Pain During Medical Procedures
Why Duration Is the Only Factor in Emotional Memory
How Medical Procedures Reveal the Limits of Modern Medicine

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: People rarely seek out news at random; they gravitate toward sources whose conclusions match the ones they already hold, and they read those sources more carefully and more charitably than ones that unsettle them. This asymmetry does not require dishonesty. A reader scanning a headline that confirms an existing view will accept it after a glance; the same reader encountering a headline that contradicts that view will pause, look for the author's credentials, and search for a competing account before accepting anything. The extra scrutiny is not applied evenly across the political spectrum; it is applied wherever the conclusion is unwelcome.

options.text: the decline of trust in professional journalism
the uneven scrutiny people apply to news that confirms or challenges their views
how political headlines are written to attract clicks
why readers prefer visual media over written articles
the history of confirmation bias research in psychology

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: Coral gets its colour, and most of its food, from a microscopic algae living inside its tissue in a relationship that has lasted for tens of millions of years. When water temperatures rise by even one or two degrees above the seasonal average for several weeks, the coral expels the algae, and with it the colour and the primary food source. The white skeleton that remains is not dead, only starving; if temperatures fall again quickly, the coral can recruit new algae and recover. Repeated bleaching events in close succession, however, leave no recovery window, and it is this repetition, more than any single event, that is now converting reefs into rubble.

options.text: the ancient origin of the algae-coral relationship
why repeated, closely spaced bleaching events are more destructive than isolated ones
methods scientists use to measure ocean temperature
the total percentage of coral reefs lost worldwide
how algae obtain energy through photosynthesis

questions.text: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
questions.context: Show a group of people a series of words related to old age—Florida, wrinkle, forgetful, bingo—embedded among neutral words, and ask them to build sentences from scrambled versions. Afterward, timed unobtrusively as they leave the building, these participants walk measurably slower down the corridor than a group given neutral words instead. None of them report noticing any theme, still less connecting it to their own pace. The mind, it turns out, does not require awareness of a cue to be shaped by it; a concept activated in one context can quietly adjust behaviour in a completely different one, without ever announcing itself to consciousness.

options.text: Walking speed is a reliable indicator of a person's true age.
Concepts activated outside conscious awareness can still influence unrelated behaviour.
Scrambled sentence tasks are the most accurate psychological measurement tool available.
People consciously adjust their behaviour once they notice an experiment's underlying theme.
Associations with old age are universally negative across all cultures studied.

questions.text: How many of the statements below do NOT agree with the passage?
questions.context:
For the first two years of learning cello, I measured myself against the other students in my youth orchestra, most of whom had started before they could read. I told myself I was simply unmusical and nearly quit twice. What changed things was a recording. My teacher had, without telling me, recorded my very first lesson, and she played it back for me during a lesson two years in. I didn't recognise the sound at first—thin, hesitant, badly out of tune—and then I realised it was me. I had improved so gradually that I had no memory of ever sounding like that. Since then, I keep a recording every few months, not to celebrate finishing anything, but so that future-me has evidence the present version of me can't see.

Statements
(a) The writer initially judged her progress by comparing herself to more experienced students.
(b) The writer seriously considered quitting the cello on more than one occasion.
(c) The writer immediately recognised her own playing in the old recording.
(d) The teacher recorded the lesson with the writer's advance knowledge and consent.
(e) The writer now records herself periodically to track long-term progress.
(f) The writer records herself in order to celebrate finishing specific pieces.

questions.text: Which statement does NOT agree with the two explanations given in the passage?
questions.context: Many island species approach humans and novel predators with little apparent fear, a phenomenon naturalists call island tameness. One explanation holds that isolation from mammalian predators over many generations has genetically selected for calmer temperaments, since vigilance that serves no purpose is metabolically wasteful and animals that spend less energy on unnecessary alarm reproduce more successfully. A second, competing explanation denies that any active selection for calmness has occurred at all; it argues that fear responses persist only where they are tested regularly by real threats, and that in their complete absence, the behaviour does not disappear through selection so much as simply fail to be maintained, drifting away from disuse rather than being selected against.

options.text: The first explanation treats calm temperament as an actively selected genetic trait.
The first explanation suggests unnecessary vigilance carries a metabolic cost.
The second explanation attributes tameness to genetic selection for calmness, identical to the first.
The second explanation suggests fear responses fade through disuse rather than active selection.
Both explanations attempt to account for the same observed pattern of reduced fear.

questions.context: Ask someone to wear an embarrassing T-shirt into a room of strangers and then estimate what percentage of people noticed it; the guess is reliably double or triple the number who actually did, according to those strangers when asked afterward. Underlying this is what researchers call _the spotlight effect_: an assumption that one's own appearance and mistakes occupy far more space in others' attention than they in fact do, because each of us is so absorbed in our own experience that we mistake that absorption for the world's.

questions.text: Which of the following questions CANNOT be answered from the passage?
questions.context: Octopuses change both the colour and the texture of their skin in under a second, using millions of pigment-filled cells called chromatophores that expand and contract under direct neural control, bypassing the slower hormonal signalling most camouflage in nature relies on. Remarkably, octopuses are colourblind; the mechanism by which they select a matching colour remains only partly understood, though researchers suspect that photoreceptor cells embedded directly in the skin itself may allow the animal to sense light without needing to see colour through its eyes at all. A disturbed octopus can also alter the texture of its skin, raising papillae to mimic the bumpy contour of coral or rock within the same instant that the colour shift occurs.

options.text: What structures allow an octopus to change skin colour so quickly?

questions.context: Decision fatigue is now a well-documented phenomenon among professionals who make many consequential choices per day. ① _Judges reviewing parole applications has been shown to grant parole far more often early in the morning than late in the afternoon, regardless of the merits of any individual case._ ② _Researchers attribute this pattern not to bias against particular defendants but to the gradual depletion of a limited mental resource._ ③ _Each decision, however small, appear to draw on the same finite reserve, whether the choice concerns parole, lunch, or a wardrobe._ ④ _This is why some highly deliberate people, most famously several well-known executives, choose to wear a near-identical outfit every day, removing one recurring decision entirely._ ⑤ _The evidence suggests that willpower behaves less like a stable character trait and more like a muscle that tires with use._

The smart-praised children, it seems, ④ _interpret_ difficulty as evidence against the very trait they were just told they possessed, and so they avoid challenges that might reveal a flaw. Praise aimed at process rather than person, by contrast, ⑤ _keeps_ the door open to continued effort.

questions.text: Among the dictionary definitions below, how many describe words that do NOT appear in the passage? (Ignore singular/plural forms, voice, and tense.)
questions.context:
Long-distance friendships are often assumed to fade through simple neglect, but researchers studying attachment have found the predominant cause lies elsewhere: people routinely overestimate how much small, regular contact matters compared to occasional, meaningful reunions. Friends who take the precaution of scheduling an annual visit, even without frequent calls between times, report closer bonds than friends who exchange frequent but shallow messages. The quality of contact, in other words, does not neatly correspond to its frequency; when old friends finally reunite in person after months apart, the relationship often resumes as though no time had passed at all.

questions.text: Which sentence best fits the blank?
questions.context: Organizational culture is often compared to an iceberg, and the comparison holds up better than most borrowed metaphors do. Above the waterline sit the artefacts anyone can observe on a single visit: the office layout, the dress code, the way meetings open and close. Below the waterline, invisible to a visitor and often only partly visible to the employees themselves, sit the assumptions that actually generate those artefacts: what the organisation believes about time, hierarchy, and whether mistakes are safe to admit. Consultants who attempt to change culture by redesigning the visible artefacts alone—new furniture, a revised dress code—routinely find the change is cosmetic and short-lived, because ________. The submerged mass, not the visible tip, determines whether a new artefact survives contact with the organisation's actual habits.

options.text: the artefacts themselves are far more expensive to redesign than the assumptions beneath them
employees generally prefer old furniture and traditional dress codes to newer alternatives
the underlying assumptions that produced the old artefacts remain untouched and simply regenerate them
consultants rarely have enough authority within a company to make any lasting changes

questions.text: Which sentence does NOT fit the overall flow of the passage?
questions.context: Many flowers that appear plain or uniformly coloured to the human eye display elaborate patterns under ultraviolet light, patterns invisible to us but perfectly visible to the bees the flowers depend on for pollination. ① These UV patterns often form a kind of runway, guiding a bee's approach directly toward the nectar and pollen at the flower's centre. ② Some patterns concentrate UV-absorbing pigment only at the base of each petal, creating a bullseye that becomes more pronounced the closer a bee gets. ③ Bees also communicate the location of food sources to other bees through a figure-eight waggle dance performed inside the hive. ④ Because the pattern is invisible to humans, plant breeders selecting for showy, human-pleasing colours have sometimes inadvertently bred flowers whose UV guides are faint or absent. ⑤ Such flowers, however visually striking to us, can be less attractive to the pollinators whose visits they still depend on for reproduction.

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate place for the given sentence: "A negotiator who opens with a number far outside any reasonable range is, perhaps counterintuitively, often more successful than one who opens moderately."
questions.context: Anchoring is among the most reliable effects in the study of judgement: an initial number, even an obviously arbitrary one, exerts measurable pull on every estimate that follows it. ( ① ) In one classic demonstration, participants spun a wheel rigged to stop at either a low or a high number, then were asked an entirely unrelated question about the percentage of African countries in the United Nations; participants who saw the high number guessed substantially higher than those who saw the low one. ( ② ) The wheel had nothing to do with the question, and participants knew it, yet the anchor pulled their estimates anyway. ( ③ ) This has obvious implications for negotiation. ( ④ ) Later offers and counteroffers tend to be adjusted from that opening anchor rather than calculated independently, so the final agreed price sits closer to the extreme opening number than a neutral analysis would predict. ( ⑤ ) The lesson is not that dishonesty pays, but that the first number spoken in any negotiation is doing more work than either party usually realises.

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate place for the given sentence: "Instead, the brain appears to store not the odor itself but the emotional and contextual scene in which it was first encountered."
questions.context: Of all the senses, smell has the strangest relationship to memory. A specific scent encountered unexpectedly can summon a memory decades old, complete with emotional intensity, faster and more vividly than a photograph or a piece of music from the same period ever could. ( ① ) Part of the explanation lies in anatomy: the olfactory bulb is only a few synapses away from the amygdala and hippocampus, the brain's centres for emotion and memory, a far shorter route than any other sense takes. ( ② ) But anatomy alone does not explain why a smell functions less like a fact retrieved and more like a scene revisited. ( ③ ) This is why the same perfume can feel neutral on one person and overwhelming on another: what is stored is not a chemical fingerprint but a specific afternoon, a specific room, a specific person, bound permanently to that molecule by the accident of when it was first inhaled. ( ④ ) No deliberate effort is required to form the link, and none is available to dissolve it afterward. ( ⑤ )

questions.text: "The rebound effect describes a curious failure of many energy-efficiency policies to deliver the savings predicted on paper." Choose the most appropriate order for the paragraphs following the given passage.

When faced with an unfamiliar problem, most people reach immediately for the most similar problem they have solved before, adapting its solution to the new case.

① This is why genuine breakthroughs so often come from outsiders to a field, who lack the established analogy and are forced to reason from the problem's actual structure instead.
② This strategy, known as analogical reasoning, is efficient precisely because it economises on effort, letting old solutions do most of the new work.
③ However, when the superficial features of a new problem resemble an old one whose deep structure is actually quite different, the borrowed solution can mislead more than it helps.

questions.context:
Color is often treated as if it were a property residing in the object itself, the way mass or volume are, but the physics tells a different story. A tomato does not contain redness; it contains a surface structure that reflects long-wavelength light more than it reflects other wavelengths, and it is a human visual system, tuned by evolution to a narrow band of that spectrum, that converts the reflected wavelength into the sensation we call red. A creature with a different visual system, encountering the identical tomato and the identical light, would have no access to that sensation at all, whatever wavelength arrived at its eye. The wavelength is objective and measurable; the redness is not out there in the world independent of a perceiving system built to generate it.

Since colour as we experience it (A) ______ the physical properties of light alone, the sensation of a particular colour (B) ________.

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate words for blanks (A) and (B).
questions.context:
Olympic bronze medalists are, on average, measurably happier in post-event interviews than silver medalists, a finding that seems to invert the actual ranking of achievement. The explanation lies not in the medal itself but in the counterfactual each athlete spontaneously compares it to. The silver medalist's mind gravitates naturally to the nearby, vivid alternative of having won gold, a single stroke away; measured against that alternative, silver feels like a loss. The bronze medalist's mind gravitates instead to the equally nearby alternative of finishing fourth and winning nothing at all; measured against that alternative, bronze feels like a win. Objective rank, in other words, predicts satisfaction far less reliably than which alternative outcome happens to come to mind.

Satisfaction with an outcome depends less on its (A) ________ rank than on the (B) ________ comparison the mind happens to generate.

options.text: (A) objective  (B) nearest counterfactual
(A) financial  (B) internationally recognised
(A) emotional  (B) least likely
(A) subjective  (B) most distant and unrealistic
(A) historical  (B) officially recorded
